title: Markel Group's Nine-Month Adjusted Operating Income Rises 14% to $707 Million as Investment Losses Turn a Year-Ago Profit Into a Comprehensive Loss
summary: Markel Group reported 2026 third-quarter and nine-month results showing 14% growth in adjusted operating income to $707.4 million and a 92% Markel Insurance combined ratio, but net investment losses of $280.9 million left the group with a comprehensive loss to shareholders of $156.3 million.
description:
Markel Group's results for the third quarter and first nine months of 2026 illustrate a point that investors in diversified insurers know well: the underlying business can improve while reported earnings move in the opposite direction. According to the company's release, the group's adjusted operating income, the measure management uses to look through market-value swings on investments, rose 14% to $707.4 million from $621.0 million a year earlier. Yet operating income under US GAAP fell to $383.2 million from $1,009.8 million, and the group recorded a comprehensive loss to shareholders of $156.3 million against comprehensive income of $793.1 million in the same period of 2025. The difference is almost entirely explained by investments.

The investment swing

Markel reported net investment losses of $280.9 million for the period, compared with net investment gains of $432.9 million a year earlier. That is a swing of roughly $714 million, which is simple arithmetic on the two reported figures, and it is larger than the entire adjusted operating income for the period. Markel carries a sizeable equity portfolio, and under GAAP the changes in the fair value of those holdings run through the income statement. When equity prices fall or fail to match a strong prior-year comparison, reported earnings fall with them, regardless of what the underwriting and operating businesses are doing. The release does not break the loss down by security or explain the market drivers in detail, so it is not possible from the source alone to say which holdings caused it.

Operating revenues still grew. The group reported operating revenues of $4,158.2 million, up 6%. That figure includes premiums earned, investment income and the revenues of the non-insurance operating businesses. The result is a company growing its top line and its adjusted profit while posting a weaker headline GAAP number, which is why management and analysts focus on the adjusted measure when assessing performance.

Underwriting: a 92% combined ratio

The Markel Insurance segment, the group's underwriting engine, produced a combined ratio of 92% for the quarter, compared with 93% a year earlier. For the nine months the combined ratio was 92% against 95%. A combined ratio below 100% means the insurer paid out less in claims and expenses than it collected in premiums, and a ratio of 92% implies roughly eight cents of underwriting profit for each dollar of premium earned. The segment's underwriting profit was $178.3 million, up 15%.

The company noted that the quarter's combined ratio included an unfavorable impact of about three points from the Global Reinsurance division, which Markel has exited. In other words, run-off effects from a business the group chose to leave still weighed on the reported ratio, which suggests the continuing business ran better than 92%. The release as published does not give catastrophe-loss or reserve-development figures, so how much of the improvement reflects benign weather, prior-year reserve movements or underlying pricing and loss trends cannot be determined from it. Readers should treat the ratio as a reported outcome rather than a full explanation of why it improved.

Earned premiums in Markel Insurance were $2.19 billion, up 3%. Underwriting gross premium volume, however, fell 9% to $2.486 billion. The company also reports an adjusted version of that metric, which strips out the effect of the exited reinsurance operations and certain business now written on a fronting basis, and on that adjusted basis underwriting gross premium volume rose 9%. The gap between a 9% reported decline and a 9% adjusted rise shows how much the group has reshaped its portfolio, and it is a good example of why comparisons of insurers' premium growth need careful definitions.

Fronting grows quickly

One of the most striking numbers in the release is fronting gross premium volume of $419 million, up 151%. In a fronting arrangement, an insurer issues policies and retains a limited share of the risk while passing most of it to reinsurers or other risk-bearing partners, earning a fee for the service. The release says Hagerty business moved to a fronting basis, which accounts for part of the increase and for part of the divergence between reported and adjusted premium volume. Fronting can generate fee income and reduce volatility, but it also depends on the credit quality and continued appetite of the partners who take the risk, and it changes how the premium numbers should be read.

Adjusted operating income for the Markel Insurance segment was $420.9 million, down 2%, even though underwriting profit rose. The release does not itemize why the two measures moved in different directions, but adjusted operating income for an insurance segment typically also reflects investment income and other items, so a rise in underwriting profit can be offset elsewhere.

The operating businesses

Beyond insurance, Markel reports the results of its other groups. Industrial adjusted operating income rose 29% to $131.1 million. The Financial group's adjusted operating income rose 30% to $80.1 million. The Consumer and Other group grew 80% to $31.2 million, a small base that magnifies percentage changes. Together these businesses help explain why group adjusted operating income grew by 14% even though the insurance segment's adjusted operating income slipped slightly. They also reflect the group's long-standing strategy of owning a range of businesses alongside its insurance operations to diversify earnings.

Capital returns

The company continued to buy back its own stock, repurchasing $315 million of shares in the third quarter and $685 million over the first nine months. At the end of the period there were 12,250 thousand shares outstanding, as stated in the release. Buybacks of that scale show management regards the shares as attractively valued after the investment-driven dip in reported earnings, though the release does not give a valuation rationale.

In the release, chief executive Tom Gayner described the company's aim as to "relentlessly compound value over the long-term", language that reflects Markel's emphasis on growth in book value and intrinsic value over quarterly earnings. That philosophy helps explain why management emphasizes adjusted operating income and long-term compounding rather than the swings in GAAP net income.

What to take from the results

For investors, brokers and policyholders, the lessons are practical. First, a specialty insurer's earnings can be dominated by investment results in any single period, so the underwriting combined ratio and adjusted operating income are better guides to the health of the insurance franchise. Second, portfolio pruning, such as exiting reinsurance and moving business to fronting, makes year-on-year premium comparisons noisy, and the adjusted figures exist for that reason. Third, strong operating-business growth can offset a flat insurance segment at the group level. Finally, a comprehensive loss in a quarter in which underwriting profit and adjusted operating income both grew is not a contradiction. It is what happens when a group holds a large investment portfolio at fair value.

Caveats apply. This article draws on a single company release, which presents management's chosen metrics. It does not include audited full-year numbers, reserve-development detail or catastrophe-loss figures, and the numbers are as reported at the time of publication. Readers who rely on Markel's results for investment decisions should consult the full financial statements and filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, and this article is not investment advice.
image_alt: Financial documents and calculator representing insurer earnings (illustrative)
key_points: Adjusted operating income rose 14% to $707.4 million from $621.0 million, while GAAP operating income fell to $383.2 million from $1,009.8 million.
Net investment losses of $280.9 million, against gains of $432.9 million a year earlier, turned comprehensive income to shareholders from a $793.1 million gain into a $156.3 million loss.
Markel Insurance reported a 92% combined ratio and underwriting profit of $178.3 million, up 15%, even as exiting the Global Reinsurance division added about three points.
Fronting gross premium volume rose 151% to $419 million, partly because Hagerty business moved to a fronting arrangement, while adjusted underwriting gross premium volume rose 9%.
Markel repurchased $315 million of stock in the quarter and $685 million year to date, and the Industrial, Financial and Consumer and Other groups all grew adjusted operating income.
why_it_matters: Markel is one of the few insurers that blends underwriting, an investment portfolio and a stable of operating businesses, so its results show how much of a specialty insurer's reported earnings can come from markets rather than from insurance. The gap between a 14% rise in adjusted operating income and a swing to a comprehensive loss is a reminder to read the components of an insurer's profit, not only the headline.

title: Heritage Insurance Reports Third-Quarter Net Income of $51.1 Million on a 73.0% Combined Ratio, With a New $50 Million Buyback Despite a 4.2% Drop in Policies
summary: Florida-based Heritage Insurance Holdings reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $51.1 million, a 73.0% net combined ratio and a 35.1% annualized return on equity, while policies in force fell 4.2% and its board authorized a new buyback of up to $50 million.
description:
Heritage Insurance Holdings, a Florida-based property insurer, reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 28 that combined strong profitability with a shrinking policy base. Net income was $51.1 million, an increase of 1.4%, and diluted earnings per share were $1.72 compared with $1.63 a year earlier. Revenues were $219.2 million. For the first nine months of the year, net income reached $149.3 million, up 15.8%, equal to earnings per share of $4.94. The company reported an annualized return on equity of 35.1% for the quarter and 36.1% for the nine months, figures that are unusually high for the insurance industry and that reflect both strong earnings and a comparatively small equity base after years of capital rebuilding.

How the combined ratio got to 73.0%

The net combined ratio for the quarter was 73.0%, composed of a loss ratio of 39.6% and an expense ratio of 33.4%. For the nine months the combined ratio was 72.9%, down from 76.8% in the same period of 2025. A combined ratio is the sum of claims and expenses as a percentage of premiums earned, so a figure of 73% indicates a substantial underwriting margin, before investment income, of about 27 cents per dollar of net premium earned. That is arithmetic on the reported ratio and not a company-stated margin.

Two items shaped the loss ratio. First, catastrophe losses were modest at $15.8 million before tax. According to the release, Hurricanes Lala and Lowell accounted for $9.1 million of that and a late-September Nor'easter for $6.7 million. Second, the company recorded favorable prior-year reserve development of $14.0 million, meaning claims from earlier years ultimately cost less than previously estimated and the reserves set aside were partly released. Lower-than-usual catastrophe activity and reserve releases both flatter a quarter, and neither is guaranteed to repeat, which is why a single strong quarter should not be extrapolated.

Premiums: smaller book, lower reinsurance cost

Gross premiums written, the total premium on policies written before reinsurance, were $322.8 million, down 3.1%. Net premiums earned, which is premium the company keeps after paying for reinsurance and recognizes as time passes, rose 5.4% to $205.6 million. The two figures moved in opposite directions largely because of the ceded premium ratio, the share of premium passed to reinsurers, which fell to 41.7% from 46.1%. Put simply, Heritage paid away a smaller portion of its premium for reinsurance, so more of each premium dollar stayed with the company.

The release also refers to the company's catastrophe excess-of-loss reinsurance program renewed in June 2026 and cites savings of $63.2 million on the program, and based on the figures given, about $36.9 million of that was recognized in 2026, though that second number is a derivation and should be treated as an estimate rather than a company-stated amount. Reinsurance costs have been among the biggest swing factors for Florida property insurers, though the release does not discuss market-wide pricing conditions.

Policy count and exposure

While profit rose, the customer base shrank. Policies in force were 347,920, a decline of 4.2%. Premiums in force, the annualized premium on those policies, were $1,399.7 million, and total insured value was $371.4 billion. The company did not explain the policy decline in the part of the release available for this article, but insurers in catastrophe-exposed states commonly reduce policy counts through underwriting actions, non-renewals, policy transfers to other carriers or competition from newer entrants. Readers should avoid assuming a specific cause. The key point is that earnings growth in the quarter did not come from adding customers; it came from lower reinsurance spending, benign catastrophe experience and reserve releases.

Balance sheet and shareholder returns

Book value per share rose 23.4% year to date to $20.22, and the debt-to-capital ratio was 10.5%. Heritage continued to return capital to shareholders. In the third quarter it bought back 100,000 shares for $3.3 million, and year to date it has repurchased 1,101,508 shares for $27.9 million. On October 28 the board approved a new repurchase program of up to $50.0 million running through December 31, 2027. The release does not mention a dividend or give earnings guidance, so investors looking for forward-looking targets will have to wait for the earnings call or other disclosures.

Chief executive Ernie Garateix described the company in the release as a "super-regional insurance carrier". The release excerpt reviewed for this article does not break down premium by state, so it is not possible here to say how much of the book is concentrated in any one state.

What the results suggest

Heritage's quarter highlights the economics of the current property insurance cycle. Heritage's own figures show strong margins helped by lower reinsurance spending and modest catastrophe losses. Conditions like these allow insurers to rebuild capital and return some of it to shareholders, as Heritage is doing. For policyholders, however, the same dynamics can mean limited competition or changes in who offers coverage, and a falling policy count at an insurer with improving profits is a sign that growth is not currently management's priority.

The risks remain clear. A concentrated catastrophe exposure means one large hurricane could erase several quarters of profit, and the reserve releases that helped this quarter could reverse if claim costs rise. Reinsurance costs could also rise at future renewals. Investors and policyholders should read the figures as a snapshot of a favorable period rather than a permanent shift.

A note on sources: this article is based on the company's own press release, which presents management's chosen figures and was only partly available for review. It is not independent analysis and it is not investment advice. Anyone considering a decision based on these results should consult the company's full filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
image_alt: Residential houses representing property insurance in the southeastern United States (illustrative)
key_points: Third-quarter net income was $51.1 million, up 1.4%, with diluted earnings per share of $1.72 against $1.63 and an annualized return on equity of 35.1%.
The net combined ratio was 73.0%, made up of a 39.6% loss ratio and a 33.4% expense ratio; catastrophe losses were $15.8 million, and prior-year reserve development was favorable by $14.0 million.
Gross premiums written fell 3.1% to $322.8 million, but a lower ceded premium ratio of 41.7% against 46.1% lifted net premiums earned 5.4% to $205.6 million.
Policies in force were 347,920, down 4.2%, and book value per share rose 23.4% year to date to $20.22.
The board approved a new repurchase program of up to $50.0 million through December 31, 2027, after the company bought back 1,101,508 shares for $27.9 million so far this year.
why_it_matters: Heritage shows how a property insurer in a catastrophe-exposed market can post very high returns while shrinking its policy count: cheaper reinsurance and a quiet storm quarter boosted margins, but the smaller book and the dependence on reinsurance costs are the points to watch. For homeowners in the region, the results show insurers are still prioritizing profitability over growth.

title: High Court Holds a Roofer's 'Reasonable Precautions' Hot-Works Condition Is Absolute, Leaving Attleys Roofing Without Cover for a School Fire Against QBE
summary: In Attleys Roofing Ltd v QBE UK Ltd [2026] EWHC 2742 (Comm), the Commercial Court ruled on October 26, 2026 that a hot works condition precedent requiring 'reasonable precautions' sets an absolute obligation, so negligence rather than recklessness can defeat an indemnity for a 2023 school fire.
description:
A short piece of punctuation sat at the centre of a High Court decision on October 26, 2026, in a case that every roofing and building contractor with a liability policy should read. In Attleys Roofing Ltd v QBE UK Ltd [2026] EWHC 2742 (Comm), the Commercial Court decided a preliminary issue about how to interpret a hot works condition in a contractor's liability policy. The question was whether an obligation to take 'reasonable precautions' is absolute, so that any failure to take them can defeat an indemnity, or whether the insurer must show something more, such as recklessness. The court held that the obligation is absolute and that negligence is enough. The reporting of the case comes from Insurance Business UK, published on October 28 and updated on October 29, and the full judgment should be read for its precise reasoning.

The fire

According to the report, the fire occurred on April 27, 2023 at a building referred to as 'the Bank' at Horris Hill Preparatory School in Newbury. Attleys had been carrying out work involving an oxyacetylene torch on lead detailing. The fire broke out after the work had finished, which is a familiar pattern with hot works: heat applied to a roof or its components can smoulder unseen and ignite materials later. QBE refused to indemnify Attleys under its Advantage Contractors Liability policy, relying on the policy's hot works condition. The dispute then went to the Commercial Court, which was asked to decide a preliminary issue on the meaning of the clause instead of trying all the facts at once.

What the clause said

The relevant provision was clause 6.5.4, which appears under the heading 'CONDITIONS PRECEDENT'. A condition precedent is a term that must be satisfied before the insurer becomes liable, and a breach can relieve the insurer of the obligation to pay the claim regardless of whether the breach caused the loss, subject to statutory limits. The clause required the policyholder to take 'reasonable precautions', with those two words placed in single inverted commas, and it listed eight specific precautions. According to the report, these included having a fire-safety person, clearing combustible material from within six metres of the work area, keeping a fire watch, and monitoring the area for one hour after hot works finished.

Attleys argued that the phrase 'reasonable precautions' made the clause something less than absolute, and it pointed to another clause, 6.5.2, which dealt with burning debris and did not use the word 'reasonable'. The argument was that the difference in wording showed the drafter intended a lower standard in clause 6.5.4, so that the insurer would need to show more than a simple failure to take care. The court was not persuaded by that contrast. According to the report, the judge described Attleys' reading as 'an unnatural reading' and noted its 'apparent illogicality'. The report says that the case of Aspen v Sangster & Annand was cited as a similar authority.

Why the ruling matters

The practical effect is that, under this wording, a contractor who fails to take the listed precautions can lose cover even if the failure was merely careless and not reckless. Policyholders often assume that an insurer must show a serious departure from standards before it can refuse a claim. The decision shows that when a policy sets out express, specific hot works precautions as a condition precedent, the court will apply them as written. The word 'reasonable' qualifies what the precautions must be, but it does not turn the duty to take them into a duty merely to try.

The decision should not be read as a ruling that QBE will win. The preliminary issue concerned interpretation only. According to the report, two matters remain undecided: whether Attleys actually breached the condition on the facts, and whether section 11 of the Insurance Act 2015 affects the insurer's reliance on it. Section 11 deals with terms designed to reduce the risk of a particular kind of loss, and it can prevent an insurer from relying on a breach where the policyholder shows that the non-compliance could not have increased the risk of the loss that actually occurred. Those points were outside the preliminary issue and will be considered later if the case continues.

Practical lessons

For contractors, the first lesson is to treat hot works conditions as obligations that must be met on every job, with records to prove it. Fire watch logs, permits, photographs of cleared work areas and sign-offs after the monitoring period can all become evidence. The second is to read the policy before starting, since a condition precedent buried in the schedule or endorsements may carry the same weight as an exclusion. The third is to speak to the broker about whether cover is available that does not depend on strict compliance, or whether a different wording would better suit the work.

For brokers, the ruling is a prompt to walk clients through hot works conditions in plain language and to check that the insured's site procedures match the policy. For insurers, it confirms that clearly drafted conditions will be enforced, although the lack of a ruling on breach and on the Insurance Act means the outcome in this case is still uncertain.

For anyone interested in how English courts approach policy wording, the case also shows the continued emphasis on the ordinary meaning of words in context. Even small drafting choices, such as quotation marks or whether one clause uses a word that another omits, are examined, but they do not override an otherwise clear obligation.

This article summarises one published report of a first-instance decision on a preliminary issue and is not legal advice. Anyone affected by a hot works condition should consult a solicitor or broker and read the full judgment.
image_alt: Building roof under repair representing roofing work and fire risk (illustrative)
key_points: The Commercial Court decided a preliminary issue on October 26, 2026 in Attleys Roofing Ltd v QBE UK Ltd [2026] EWHC 2742 (Comm).
The hot works condition, clause 6.5.4 of the Advantage Contractors Liability policy, sits under the heading 'CONDITIONS PRECEDENT' and places 'reasonable precautions' in single inverted commas.
The court held the obligation is absolute, so a failure caused by negligence can defeat cover; the insurer does not have to show recklessness.
The fire broke out on April 27, 2023 at a building known as 'the Bank' at Horris Hill Preparatory School near Newbury, after oxyacetylene torch work on lead detailing had finished.
Whether Attleys actually breached the condition, and whether section 11 of the Insurance Act 2015 limits QBE's defence, remain to be decided.
why_it_matters: Contractors who carry out hot works rely on liability cover that can be lost entirely if a precaution wording is breached. The ruling shows that courts will read a clearly drafted condition precedent according to its words, and that punctuation and heading can matter. Brokers and insureds should check hot works conditions before work begins, not after a loss.

title: IAG's FY26 Profit Reached A$1.02 Billion After 109 Weather Events, While Its Bid for RAC WA Now Hinges on a Competition Tribunal Process
summary: Insurance Australia Group reported FY26 net profit after tax of A$1.022 billion on A$18.4 billion of gross written premium after 109 weather events, and is separately trying to save its RAC Western Australia deal by offering NRMA renewal rights and resilience commitments to the ACCC.
description:
Insurance Australia Group, the country's largest general insurer, closed its 2026 financial year with a profit that came despite a long list of weather events, and it now faces a regulatory test over its planned purchase of RAC Insurance in Western Australia. The two stories are linked: the first shows the strength of IAG's underlying business, and the second shows how much that business wants to grow by acquisition. The facts below come from Insurance Business Australia reports published on October 14 and October 23, 2026. IAG disclosed its results to the Australian Securities Exchange on August 13, so the figures are not new, but the reporting adds useful detail on claims and on the competition process.

A year of weather

According to the October 23 report, IAG responded to 109 weather events during FY26, 65 in Australia and 44 in New Zealand, and paid A$12.4 billion of claims. Its net natural perils cost was A$1.169 billion, which was below its allowance of A$1.216 billion. Cyclone Alfred in March 2026 added roughly A$200 million to the cost, and the Australian Reinsurance Pool Corporation, the government-backed terrorism and cyclone reinsurance pool, paid out more than A$1 billion in connection with it. The Insurance Council of Australia estimated insured losses at A$4.8 billion in calendar year 2025, which gives context for the scale of the industry's exposure.

Staying under the natural perils allowance is notable because insurers set aside a budget for weather, and a result inside that budget supports margins. On the reported figures, the weather costs, though large in absolute terms, came in slightly below what IAG had allowed for.

The headline numbers

The group reported net profit after tax of A$1.022 billion, gross written premium of A$18.4 billion and an insurance profit of A$1.6 billion. The underlying margin was 15.0%, with a reported margin of 14.7%. Intermediated gross written premium, the business sold through brokers and other intermediaries, rose 1.1% to A$4.6 billion, while direct premium reached A$10.3 billion, up 17.8%. Excluding the RACQ business, which IAG acquired in September 2025, direct premium growth was about 4.5%. That adjustment shows that much of the direct growth came from an acquisition rather than from organic expansion.

Executives spoke about the commercial market and about technology. Jarrod Hill, chief executive of CGU and WFI, described commercial insurance as cyclical, in comments the source summarises only briefly. Chief executive Nick Hawkins said that use of artificial intelligence had passed 80% and pointed to momentum into FY27. The company said its intermediated business was well above its A$250 million insurance profit target.

For FY27 the guidance is gross written premium growth of 5% to 8% and a reported insurance margin of 14.5% to 16.5%. Its longer-term Ambition 2030 targets more than 11 million customers and more than A$25 billion of gross written premium.

The RAC Western Australia deal

IAG's plan to acquire RAC's insurance business in Western Australia is the most visible test of its growth strategy. According to the October 14 report, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, which since January 1, 2026 has operated under a mandatory merger regime, opposed the transaction. The report says that, on the ACCC's analysis, IAG would hold about 55% to 65% of Western Australian motor insurance and 50% to 60% of home and contents insurance, which the commission regards as a concentrated position.

In response, IAG lodged a public benefits application and offered a set of commitments. The first and most striking is an offer to transfer renewal rights on active NRMA Western Australia home and motor policies, effectively handing part of its existing customer base to another insurer so that the combined business would not become as dominant. IAG also offered to improve the availability of RAC home insurance north of the 26th parallel, which includes towns such as Karratha, Port Hedland and Broome, where cover can be hard to find. It proposed to invest A$20 million in Western Australian resilience over ten years and said it would accept stronger measures if pricing breaches occur.

IAG says the acquisition would add about A$1.2 billion to annual gross written premium, would be accretive to earnings per share in the first full year, and would produce about A$100 million of annual pre-tax synergies, at a cost of A$15 million to A$25 million a year in integration costs for three years. Those are the company's own estimates and have not been independently verified here.

The process

Applications to the Competition Tribunal were lodged on October 1 and October 5, with a hearing on October 8, according to the report. Filing a public benefits application suspends the ACCC's timetable, and the commission has 50 business days to consider it. IAG has said it expects completion in December 2026. Whether that holds will depend on the ACCC's decision and any further tribunal step.

What to watch

For Western Australian customers, the outcome determines how many choices they have for home and motor cover and how much pricing discipline the market will see. The renewal-rights offer is a signal that IAG is willing to give up some customers to win approval, and the commitment on cover in the north responds to a long-standing concern about availability in cyclone-exposed regions. For the wider industry, the case is an early example of how the new merger rules apply to insurance, and the result may influence how future deals are structured.

This article summarises two trade-press reports and the company's disclosed figures. It is not investment or legal advice, and readers who want to rely on the numbers should refer to IAG's ASX filings and the ACCC's published materials.

key_points: IAG reported FY26 net profit after tax of A$1.022 billion on gross written premium of A$18.4 billion, with an insurance profit of A$1.6 billion and an underlying margin of 15.0%.
The group responded to 109 weather events (65 in Australia, 44 in New Zealand) and paid A$12.4 billion of claims; net natural perils cost was A$1.169 billion against an allowance of A$1.216 billion.
FY27 guidance is for gross written premium growth of 5% to 8% and a reported insurance margin of 14.5% to 16.5%.
To save its acquisition of RAC Insurance in Western Australia, IAG offered to transfer renewal rights on active NRMA WA home and motor policies after the ACCC opposed the deal.
IAG says the RAC deal would add about A$1.2 billion of annual premium and about A$100 million of annual pre-tax synergies, and it expects completion in December 2026 if approved.
why_it_matters: IAG's results show how an insurer can earn a strong profit in a year of heavy weather by pricing and reinsuring for it, while the RAC dispute shows how competition law now shapes insurance mergers in Australia. Western Australian drivers and homeowners are the ones whose choice of insurer would change if the deal proceeds.

title: France's First Insurability Observatory Report Finds No Commune Without Home Insurance, but 811 Communes Show Tension and Climate Costs Are Heading Toward €4 Billion a Year
summary: The first report of France's Observatoire de l'assurabilité, delivered in June 2026, found that every commune has at least one insurer for single-family homes and 97.7% of mainland communes are normal, but 811 show light or moderate tension, prompting a government plan to adapt the Cat Nat system.
description:
France has run a national natural-disaster compensation scheme since 1982, and in June 2026 it published its first systematic assessment of whether homeowners can still obtain cover as climate risks rise. The Observatoire de l'assurabilité, whose first report was delivered on June 15, 2026, was produced with the state-owned reinsurer Caisse centrale de réinsurance, known as CCR. On June 22 the government set out its response. This article draws on the Direction générale du Trésor's summary and the press kit published by the ecological transition ministry. Because both documents date from June, the article reflects the position at that time and should not be read as current to October.

How the scheme works

The Cat Nat regime obliges insurers to include natural-disaster cover in home and motor policies, funded by a surcharge on premiums, once the government has declared an event a natural disaster by decree. CCR offers reinsurance on the scheme, and the state provides an unlimited guarantee. According to the report, average annual claims were about €1 billion between 1982 and 2024. They are now close to €2 billion and are projected to reach about €4 billion a year by 2050. The drought of 2022, which damaged buildings through clay soils shrinking and swelling, cost more than €3.5 billion on its own. The rising cost trend is the context for a standing instrument to track whether cover remains available.

What the Observatory measured

The report covers single-family homes in mainland France and in Guadeloupe, Martinique, La Réunion, Saint-Martin and Saint-Barthélemy. It examines floods, drought linked to clay soil movement and, for the overseas territories only, cyclones. It measures availability by counting the insurers willing to cover homes in each commune and classifies communes as normal, or under light, moderate or high tension. By the report's definition, a commune with 1,000 houses is under light tension if fewer than 25 insurers are willing to insure it and under moderate tension if fewer than 23 are.

The headline result is reassuring on its face. Every commune has at least one insurer. In mainland France, 97.7% of communes are classed as normal. A total of 811 communes, just over 2% of the mainland total, show some tension: 568, or 1.6%, are under light tension and 243, or 0.7%, under moderate tension. None is classified red, the most severe category. The situation overseas is different: all the territories studied show moderate tension, which means the choice of insurers is narrower than on the mainland.

These thresholds measure how many insurers are willing to cover, not what customers pay or whether claims are settled quickly. A commune can be classed as normal and still have rising premiums or higher deductibles, and a count of insurers does not by itself capture affordability. That is a limit on how far the numbers can be read. Ministers asked for the report to be produced annually.

The government's response

On June 22 the government, through ministers including Monique Barbut and Roland Lescure, said it would adapt the system rather than wait for tension to spread. The Direction générale du Trésor summary lists several actions. An inter-ministerial mission will examine the overseas territories, where the tension is greatest. The Cat Nat surcharge will be reviewed every five years so that the funding of the scheme keeps pace with the cost of claims. The government also intends to keep insurers present in exposed zones and to ease access to the Bureau central de tarification, the body that can require an insurer to cover a risk it has refused. Ministers also asked for the report to be produced annually.

The ministry's press kit adds prevention measures. It mentions a clay experiment running since September 2025 in 11 departments, new rules for building on clay soils for construction from July 1, the integration of the national climate adaptation reference trajectory into flood prevention plans, a national flood map from the Cerema technical agency to be published after the summer, and an evaluation of a flood-resilience programme at the end of June. The details of each measure are in the primary documents and are summarised here only briefly.

What it means for homeowners and insurers

For homeowners, the first finding is that cover is generally available, so there is no immediate gap in the system. The second is that the system is under pressure from rising claims, particularly from drought and floods, and from the cost of rebuilding. That pressure usually reaches households through higher premiums, changes in surcharges or stricter underwriting in the most exposed areas. The commitment to review the surcharge every five years signals that the government expects costs to keep rising.

For insurers, the report creates a transparent benchmark. If the number of communes under tension increases, the benchmark will show it. The emphasis on prevention suggests the government sees reducing damage as part of the answer alongside funding. For overseas territories, where tension is already moderate everywhere, the planned mission is likely to be the most closely watched part of the response.

How to read the numbers

The percentages describe a snapshot, and they rely on the definitions chosen by the Observatory. They apply to single-family homes and not to apartments, commercial property or vehicles. The projection of about €4 billion a year by 2050 is an estimate and depends on assumptions about climate and exposure. Later reports will show whether the trend is stable.

This article summarises official French publications dated June 2026. It is general information and not insurance or legal advice, and anyone seeking cover or challenging a refusal should consult their insurer, broker or the relevant French authority.
source_name: Direction générale du Trésor (June 22, 2026) and French Ministry of Ecological Transition press kit
image_alt: French town houses representing home insurance availability (illustrative)
key_points: The first Observatoire de l'assurabilité report, prepared by the state reinsurer CCR and delivered on June 15, 2026, found that 100% of communes have at least one insurer for single-family homes.

In mainland France, 97.7% of communes are classed as normal, 243 (0.7%) show moderate tension and 568 (1.6%) show light tension, a total of 811; none is classed red, while all studied overseas areas show moderate tension.

Average Cat Nat claims were about €1 billion a year from 1982 to 2024, are now close to €2 billion and are projected to reach about €4 billion a year by 2050; the 2022 drought alone cost more than €3.5 billion.

On June 22 the government proposed an inter-ministerial mission on overseas territories, a review of the Cat Nat surcharge every five years, measures to keep insurers present in exposed zones and more prevention.
This article reports a June 2026 publication and the first annual assessment, so later developments are not covered.
why_it_matters: France's natural-disaster scheme is one of Europe's best-known public-private models, and its first systematic measure of whether homeowners can still find cover is an early-warning tool for climate change. The finding that availability is widely intact but strained in about 2% of communes and in overseas territories frames the policy choices that will determine premiums and access.

title: Japan's Life Insurers Clear the New J-ICS Solvency Bar: Nippon Life Reports a 195% Ratio, Daiichi Life About 220%, as the 100% Minimum Replaces the Old 200% Test
summary: Japan's economic-value-based solvency regime, aligned with the IAIS Insurance Capital Standard, took effect for the year ended March 2026 with a 100% minimum; Fitch says major insurers clear it comfortably, with Nippon Life at 195% consolidated and Daiichi Life at about 220%.
description:
Japan's insurance supervisors completed one of the most significant changes to the country's financial regulation in years when an economic-value-based solvency regime took effect for the fiscal year that ended in March 2026. Known as J-ICS, it replaced the old solvency margin ratio. The first set of results, reported by Insurance Business Asia on July 28, 2026 and drawn from a podcast by Fitch Ratings recorded on July 23, suggests that the largest life and non-life insurers have cleared the new bar with room to spare. This article summarises those results and the context, and it is limited to what the cited report says.

What changed

Under the earlier regime, insurers were measured on the solvency margin ratio, which was based largely on book values and had a regulatory floor of 200%. The new economic solvency ratio, or ESR, values assets and liabilities on a market-consistent basis and sets a minimum of 100%. The headline numbers are therefore not directly comparable: a ratio of 195% under the new system does not mean the same as a ratio of 195% under the old one, and the lower numerical minimum does not mean the rules are looser. According to Fitch, the regime is conservative, in part because the stress for mass policy lapses is calibrated to conditions in the UK and Europe, which can be harsher than Japanese experience.

J-ICS is designed to align with Solvency II, the European regime, and with the Insurance Capital Standard developed by the International Association of Insurance Supervisors. The IAIS finalised its standard in December 2024. The report notes that self-assessments are being carried out in 2026 and that targeted assessments are due to begin from 2027. Aligning with international standards is intended to make Japanese insurers' capital comparable with their overseas peers and to support cross-border business.

The first results

Nippon Life, the country's largest life insurer, reported a regulatory ESR of 195% on a consolidated basis and 204% on a non-consolidated basis. The consolidated figure fell because the company consolidated Resolution Life, the acquisition of which was completed on October 30, 2025 for around US$8.4 billion for the remaining stake of about 77%, valuing Resolution Life at about US$10.6 billion. The company's medium-term target range is 200% to 270%, so the consolidated ratio sits just below the bottom of that range after the acquisition. The report links the lower consolidated figure to the Resolution Life consolidation.

Daiichi Life's group ESR was about 220%, an increase of about 10 percentage points. Tokio Marine reported 268%, a figure aligned with the international standard. According to the report, MS&AD, Sompo and Tokio Marine all reported ratios above 200%. Taken together, the results indicate that large Japanese insurers are well above the 100% minimum, though the report does not list ratios for every company.

The sector's profitability supports that picture. The Financial Services Agency reported that the 21 major life insurers earned net income of ¥2.54 trillion, up from ¥2.29 trillion a year earlier. The source does not link that profit to the solvency ratios directly.

New instruments and supervisory concerns

One consequence of the new regime is the arrival of a new type of capital instrument. The report mentions holding-company Tier 2 senior debt as a new instrument that insurers can use to strengthen capital. Such instruments give groups another route to raise regulatory capital, but investors will price them according to their structure and the group's credit quality.

The report also notes that supervisors, including the FSA and the IAIS, are paying attention to alternative assets and to asset-intensive reinsurance, in which insurers transfer blocks of business and related assets to reinsurers. Life insurers worldwide have increased their holdings of private credit and other alternative assets in search of yield, and regulators want to be sure that capital rules capture the risks. How Japanese supervisors will apply that scrutiny is not detailed in the source.

Why the size of the market matters

Japan accounts for around 5% of the global insurance market, with about US$363 billion of premiums in 2024. Japanese life insurers are also active overseas buyers, as the Nippon Life and Resolution Life deal shows. A solvency regime that is internationally aligned shapes how those insurers are measured against overseas peers when they deploy capital abroad.

Overlap with earlier coverage

PolicyRix has previously reported on Fitch's view of the three largest Japanese insurance groups, which also mentioned ratios above 200% and Tokio Marine's 268%. This article differs in focusing on the life insurers and the framework itself, but readers will notice that some figures recur because they come from the same Fitch commentary.

Limits of the report

The source is a trade-press summary of a podcast, so the underlying company disclosures and Fitch's written research should be consulted for detail. Ratios are reported by the companies and may be restated. Differences between consolidated and non-consolidated measures, and between regulatory and internally defined ratios, mean that comparisons between insurers need care. This article is general information, not investment advice.
source_name: Insurance Business Asia (July 28, 2026), citing a Fitch Ratings podcast
image_alt: Tokyo skyline representing Japanese life insurers (illustrative)
key_points: Japan's new economic-value-based solvency regime, known as J-ICS, replaced the old solvency margin ratio from the fiscal year ended March 2026 and sets a minimum economic solvency ratio of 100%, against the previous 200% floor.
Nippon Life reported a regulatory ratio of 195% consolidated and 204% non-consolidated, lower after consolidating Resolution Life, with a medium-term target range of 200% to 270%.
Daiichi Life's group ratio was about 220%, up about 10 points, while Tokio Marine reported 268% on a basis aligned with the international standard; MS&AD, Sompo and Tokio Marine were all above 200%.
Fitch describes J-ICS as conservative, in part because the mass-lapse stress is calibrated to UK and European conditions.
The regime is aligned with Solvency II and the IAIS Insurance Capital Standard, and regulators are watching alternative assets and asset-intensive reinsurance.
why_it_matters: A solvency regime determines how much capital an insurer must hold and how much risk it can take, so the switch to an economic-value basis affects Japan's roughly US$363 billion annual premium market and how Japanese insurers compare with overseas peers. The first set of results suggests the transition has been smooth, but the lower ratios at some firms and the new debt instruments are worth watching.
